article.name: Flair
article.summary: Flair is a self-hosted agent identity and memory service built as a native Harper application. It stores agent memories in Harper/RocksDB, creates embeddings in process, and combines vector and lexical retrieval. This is a source-based review; no system behavior or performance was measured.

who_what.text: The current README presents Flair as an open-source, self-hosted identity and memory substrate for agents, with a CLI, Harper server, MCP integrations, client libraries, and framework bridges. This review covers its memory service and adjacent scope controls; it does not establish a complete maintainer roster.

The repository describes Flair as a native Harper application. Harper provides HTTP handling and persistence in one process, backed by RocksDB; the project says it does not require a separate vector database or embedding API.

architecture.text: The Memory table stores an owner agent ID, text, visibility, durability, timestamps, optional temporal validity and supersession fields, archive state, provenance, and usage/search counters. The schema declares an HNSW index on its embedding column; relationships are represented separately as temporal subject-predicate-object records.

For local semantic retrieval, the README documents in-process nomic-embed-text-v1.5 embeddings with 768 dimensions on CPU or supported GPU. Harper persists the vectors alongside records; the service also uses a lexical BM25 index and fuses lexical and vector candidates with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF).

The semantic endpoint filters candidates by read scope, archive state, and optional tag, subject, time, and score constraints. It over-fetches candidates before returning the requested limit, and offers optional explain-plan and per-leg candidate diagnostics.

MCP exposes memory_store, memory_search, memory_update, memory_get, and memory_delete among other tools. The README describes local stdio clients and a separate native OAuth-backed /mcp endpoint, which is off by default.

behavior.text: **Write.** Authenticated agent writes are attributed to the caller and restricted to its own rows. Memory writes are auto-embedded when the local embedding path is available; server-controlled fields include provenance timestamps and row-incarnation metadata. Durability defaults to standard; omitted visibility defaults to private for standard or ephemeral memories and shared for permanent or persistent memories. The CLI and MCP/API surfaces expose memory_store.

**Update and correction.** Memory update uses a read-modify-write flow that can update a record in place or create a successor using `supersedes`; the successor chain and validFrom/validTo fields represent revisions and temporal validity. Maintenance can archive expired standard memories and reap expired ephemeral ones; these lifecycle labels do not imply backup or replica acknowledgements.

**Delete and archive.** Owner or admin `DELETE /Memory/<id>` is the user-facing delete operation; permanent-memory deletion may append deletion history. Basement/archive sets an archive flag and can be reversed, retaining the row. Physical purge is a separate operator/internal operation with post-commit confirmation; agent keys, including admin-agent keys, do not authorize it.

**Retrieval.** The default retrieval mode is hybrid BM25 plus vector candidates fused by RRF, with vector-only and BM25-only modes also represented in source. Search supports filters and optional trust evidence or abstention; these options are opt-in. The displayed semantic similarity is a ranking signal, not a calibrated probability of answering correctly.

**Scope isolation.** A verified non-admin reader can read all of its own memories and other agents' non-private memories on the same instance. `private` is the owner-only visibility; missing visibility is treated as non-private for legacy rows. Writes are isolated to the authenticated owner. Admin and trusted in-process reads have broader access, while federation applies an inter-instance boundary. This is an open shared knowledge model within one instance, not strict per-agent read isolation.

**Provenance and evidence.** Local writes stamp a server-derived verified agent and receipt time in provenance, while caller-supplied model/client or claimed creation-time fields remain claims. Search can expose provenance and optional trust context; trust metadata informs the reader and is not an authorization decision. The schema also supports source pointers and usage signals. These records aid traceability but do not establish that a memory is true or that an answer is entailed by it.

**Efficiency and observability.** The code uses HNSW vector retrieval, a bounded BM25 candidate window and RRF fusion, scope-aware candidate filtering, selected-field projections, and batched source-pointer joins. Search-hit counts are written to a separate MemoryHitStat table rather than rewriting memory rows for every hit; a distinct usageCount records explicit use feedback. Explain mode and optional retrieval-leg output expose query/candidate diagnostics. These are design observations, not measured latency, throughput, or storage results.

metrics.evidence: Hybrid retrieval and an opt-in abstention path are present in source; no answers were scored.
In-place and successor updates plus temporal validity are represented; no correction sequence or stale-value probe was run.
Owner delete, archival, and operator purge are documented; no post-delete recall or index cleanup workload was run.
The source defines open-within-instance reads with a private-owner exception; no cross-agent or cross-instance isolation workload was measured.
Provenance and optional trust/source information are exposed; no generated answer claims were adjudicated against cited memories.
The source describes vector and lexical retrieval paths but this review collected no timings.
No workload token counts, charges, or corpus-attributable storage measurements were collected.

limits.text: This bounded review inspected the current README, API and access-control docs, Memory schema, centralized scope, memory CRUD/archive/purge, retrieval, ranking, and hit-tracking source at the verified main SHA. Flair, its tests, and benchmarks were not run.

The docs state that the system is self-hosted and that memory data is not encrypted with the agent signing key. Deployment security, backups, restore behavior, key operations, and production configuration were not exercised in this review.

The open-within-instance read policy permits any verified agent to read another agent's non-private memories. Whether this is suitable depends on instance trust and visibility choices; federation and private visibility do not turn all same-instance reads into tenant isolation.

Source structure and project-published retrieval examples do not establish recall quality, abstention calibration, correctness of provenance, deletion leakage, scope safety under a workload, concurrency outcomes, latency, cost, or storage efficiency. These remain unknown here.

benchmark.note: No Flair runtime, tests, or benchmarks were run. Source observations and upstream-published figures are not results from this project's benchmark.
